analysis.one_liner: Overrides state laws requiring overtime pay for farmworkers beyond 60 hours a week.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote in the House Education and Workforce Committee before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law currently does not require overtime pay for farmworkers. Some states, notably New York, have stepped in and set their own weekly hour limits that trigger overtime for agricultural workers. This bill would wipe out any state law that sets a farm workweek shorter than 60 hours before overtime kicks in, meaning state protections stronger than 60 hours would disappear. It died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Farm operators, especially dairy and other labor-intensive growers in states like New York, would avoid paying overtime when their employees work long weeks, keeping labor costs lower. Their employees would be the ones working those longer weeks without extra pay.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Farm operators in states with overtime laws

how_it_helps.text: The bill preempts any state law that sets a maximum agricultural workweek shorter than 60 hours, removing state-mandated overtime pay for farmworkers in those states.
Under federal law, agricultural employees are generally exempt from overtime requirements, so state laws are currently the only source of farmworker overtime protections in most places.
The bill would change the Fair Labor Standards Act so that federal law preempts those state laws, leaving farmwork exempt from overtime once again.

analysis.who_pays: Farmworkers in states with overtime protections would lose them, working more than 60 hours a week with no overtime premium. Taxpayers and communities bear no direct cost, but the workers' earnings would fall for the same hours.
analysis.who_pays_short: Farmworkers in states with overtime rules

drawbacks.text: The bill would eliminate overtime pay that state legislatures chose to give farmworkers, reducing earnings for people who often work very long hours.

Farm operators argue that state overtime mandates raise costs sharply in labor-intensive agriculture like dairying, and that a uniform 60-hour federal threshold prevents a patchwork where workers or operations move to states with weaker rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gain goes to farm operators in lower labor costs; the cost falls on farmworkers who lose overtime pay they currently receive under state law. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how much of the cost farmers can absorb versus pass on, but the bill does not offer workers any compensation for the protections it removes.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Brandon Williams of New York introduced the bill on January 12, 2023, joined by four New York Republican colleagues as original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day and saw no further action.
Seventeen Republicans in total cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
The bill never left committee, so state agricultural overtime laws remained in effect through the 118th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Farmworkers in states with overtime protections kept their current rights, because the bill died in committee without changing federal law. Farm operators did not get the state overtime mandates preempted, so they continue to pay overtime in those states.

for.name: Rep. Brandon Williams
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited four New York Republican colleagues as original cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 recorded supporters, the sponsor and 17 cosponsors, were Republicans; no Democrat supported it, but the bill never advanced far enough to force a floor vote that would show the full split.

industries.industry: Farm operators (especially dairy and other labor-intensive agriculture)
industries.note: The bill would relieve them of state overtime mandates that currently apply when employees exceed 60 hours in a week, cutting payroll costs in states like New York. The saving comes directly out of farmworkers' overtime earnings.

Farmworkers are the people whose pay the bill would reduce: they would work the same long weeks without the overtime premium state law currently provides. Because federal law exempts farmwork from overtime, state laws are their main protection.
